prompt:
I run a pottery studio (Kiln & Co., about 40 members) and I want something to put up on the screen at our staff meeting Thursday: what it's like to become a member, from the first time someone Googles us to around their third month. Here's what I got from chatting to six new members over the last month:

- Most found us through a friend's Instagram post or a local search. Two almost didn't come because the class times on our site were out of date.
- The trial class is $35 and nearly everyone loved it. They said the teacher made them feel like it was okay to be bad at it.
- After the trial, the membership options page confused four of the six. They weren't sure whether the monthly plan included glaze and firing.
- Two joined on the spot at the front desk. Four went home to think about it. One of those never got a follow-up email and only joined because a friend nudged her.
- First month: they love the open studio hours, but three felt like they were in the way of the regulars, and two couldn't figure out the shelf system for unfinished pieces.
- Firing takes 2 to 3 weeks and nobody told two of them that, so they thought their pieces were lost.
- Two were thinking of not renewing at month three because of time, one because she felt she wasn't getting better.

One self-contained HTML file please, inline CSS, no external stuff.
rubric: One page that covers the whole span in time order, from the first search to about month three, so the sequence is readable at a glance.
It is clearly about one kind of person (a new member), and what that person does, thinks and feels at each stage comes from the six conversations rather than generic wording.

The bad moments are visibly marked (out-of-date class times, confusing plan page, no follow-up, unexplained firing wait, feeling in the regulars' way, month-three doubt), and the high of the trial class shows too, so the page is not an even stream of positive feelings.
It shows something the studio itself does or owns at those points (website hours, follow-up email, firing schedule, shelf system, front desk), so staff can see what to change.
No invented figures, quotes or findings beyond what was supplied: counts match the six people and it does not claim to speak for all members.
In the screenshot the text is legible at screen size and the page is not crammed.

prompt:
My team made this for our meal-kit business and I have to present it to the VP next week. Be straight with me, is it any good?

Persona: Busy Brenda, 34, marketing manager, loves cooking, short on time

Awareness: Sees an Instagram ad. Feeling: Curious 😀
Consideration: Visits website, reads reviews, compares us to competitors. Feeling: Interested 😀
Purchase: Picks a plan and checks out. Feeling: Excited 😀
Onboarding: Receives first box, unpacks. Feeling: Happy 😀
Usage: Cooks the meals. Feeling: Satisfied 😀
Retention: Gets emails and offers. Feeling: Loyal 😀
Advocacy: Refers friends. Feeling: Delighted 😀

Opportunities: Improve personalization, enhance the app, increase engagement.
rubric: Says plainly that it is not ready to present, rather than opening with praise or a balanced shrug.
Points out that the feelings never dip and are never explained, so the map cannot show where anything goes wrong.
Notes that nothing shows where any of it came from (no customers, data or staff input), that the persona looks assumed, and says what to add.

Notes that the stages follow the company's sales funnel instead of what the customer lives through week to week, and that real trouble spots such as skipping a week, a box that doesn't fit the week, or cancelling are missing, as is anything the company does out of the customer's sight.
Notes that the opportunities are generic and not tied to any moment on the map.
Gives a short, ordered list of what to fix first that could be done before next week.

prompt: I own a physio clinic with three locations. Roughly a third of new patients don't come back after their first appointment and our front desk says the referral paperwork is a mess. My manager wants "a map of the whole patient experience" by the end of the month. I have two admins and a few hours from one therapist, and no budget. Where should I actually start and what should the thing look like? I haven't talked to any patients yet.
rubric: Recommends a narrow scope tied to the actual problem (for example referral through to the second appointment) rather than the whole patient experience, and says why.
Says whose experience it follows (a newly referred patient) and that the front desk and referral paperwork work belongs in the picture, not only what the patient sees.

Names what to base it on within their means (a handful of short conversations with patients who did and did not return, front desk and therapist walk-throughs, the appointment data they already have) and is honest that without patient input the map would be guesswork.
Gives a plan that fits two admins, a few therapist hours and a month, not a long programme.
Names specific moments in this clinic (referral arrives, first call to schedule, intake forms, first session, booking the next visit) instead of a generic lecture.

prompt: Need two or three sentences, 70 words max, I'm pasting it into an email to our CFO. Why would she approve two weeks of my team's time to map everything that happens, in front of the customer and behind the scenes, when someone returns something they bought from our online homewares store? She's skeptical of "design exercises".
rubric: 70 words or fewer, in plain prose without headings or bullets.
Ties the work to money and operations in returns (cost per return, repeat purchases, staff time, handoffs between teams) in words a finance person uses, with no design jargon.
Says concretely what two weeks produces (a picture of where returns break, who handles each step, and which fixes to do first), not empathy or alignment.
Does not promise a specific saving or invent figures.

prompt:
We looked at what it's like to move a parent into our assisted-living home, from the first tour to the end of week six. I need a short message (under 200 words) to our leadership team for Monday that says what we found and what I want them to do about it. Use only this:

- We followed 5 families (adult children) through the process and talked to 4 staff.
- All 5 families said the tour was great; the sales coordinator is the reason.
- 4 of the 5 families didn't know who to call between signing and move-in, about three weeks.
- Getting the medication list from the family's doctor takes our nurses 2 to 3 days of phone chasing per resident. Nobody had measured it before.
- In week one, 3 of the 5 parents ate most meals alone in their room. The dining team didn't know the new resident had arrived.
- Two staff said the move-in checklist is a Word file last updated two years ago.
- At Tuesday's leadership meeting I want one named owner for each of the first three gaps.
rubric: Uses only the supplied facts: no invented percentages, counts, quotes or outcomes, and counts stay as "4 of 5" or are flagged as a small group of five families rather than stretched to "most residents".
Opens with what the leadership team needs to decide or do, not with how the work was done.
Picks the moments that matter (nobody to call between signing and move-in, the medication list chase, week-one meals) and treats the tour as a strength to protect.
States the ask clearly: a named owner for each of the first three gaps at Tuesday's meeting.
Under 200 words, plain wording, no consulting jargon.

prompt:
I'm presenting this to the library board tomorrow. It's from our work on the Saturday toddler story hour. Anything you'd change before I walk in?

Who: a parent new to the area with one toddler (age 2) who has never used our library; came on a Saturday after seeing the flyer at the pediatrician. Based on 8 short exit interviews and 3 Saturdays of watching the door, April to May.

Before: Sees the flyer at the pediatrician and wonders if it's free and whether a non-member can come. Feels: unsure. [8 of 8 asked staff or looked online for "is it free"; the website doesn't say]
Arrival: Parks in the rear lot, can't tell which door is open on Saturdays. Feels: flustered. [watched 5 parents try the locked front door first]
Story hour: Finds the room, toddler settles, the librarian's songs are the high point. Feels: relieved, then happy. [7 of 8 named the songs unprompted]
After: Wants to borrow a picture book, but the sign-up needs ID with a local address and new residents often don't have one yet. Feels: embarrassed. [3 of 8 left without borrowing]
Behind the scenes: front desk staff are trained for members; nobody is assigned to the Saturday door; the card form is paper only.

Opportunities, in order: 1) say "free, no sign-up" on the flyer and the website; 2) a sign on the front door pointing to the rear entrance on Saturdays; 3) accept a utility bill or a temporary card for new residents.
Owners: marketing, facilities, branch manager. First check-in: June board meeting.
rubric: Says it is in good shape and that only small changes are warranted; it does not rebuild or restructure it.
Leaves the stages, evidence tags, behind-the-scenes line and the order of opportunities essentially intact, and adds no new sections, columns or frameworks.
Offers at most a few specific, minor suggestions tied to the text (for example, being upfront that eight interviews is a small group), each saying where it goes.
Does not invent new findings, numbers or fixes beyond what is on the page.
Is short, and adds a sentence or two of practical help for the presentation itself, such as what to ask the board for.

prompt: Can you write the steps for our help page on changing the delivery address in our grocery app? What I know: you open Account, then Addresses, tap the address you want to change, edit it, and tap Save. If an order is already being picked, the change only applies to the next order.
rubric: A short numbered list of steps in the order given, in plain wording a customer can follow.
Includes the caveat that an order already being picked keeps the old address and the change applies to the next one.
Stays a help-page answer: no stages, feelings, opportunities, back-office layers or other mapping apparatus, and no invented screens, buttons or timings.
Short: roughly 120 words or fewer.

prompt: We sell a monthly pet-food subscription and keep losing people around month 2 to 4. This is what I have. 31 cancellation survey answers: dog wouldn't eat the new recipe 11, price after the intro discount ended 9, too much food piling up 6, other 5. From support tickets, the common ones are "how do I skip a delivery" (people can't find it) and "my box came on a day I'm not home". Can you lay out the customer journey for me so I can show the team where it's going wrong?
rubric: Centres on the stretch where people leave (the first box through about month four) instead of padding it out with generic stages from first hearing about the brand to referring friends.
Ties each moment to the supplied evidence (recipe refusal, price when the intro discount ends, food piling up, skip hard to find, delivery day) with the counts quoted correctly out of 31.
Says what this evidence cannot show (only people who cancelled answered; nothing from those who stay; feelings are inferred from reasons and tickets) and what would fill the gap, briefly.
Includes what the company does or controls at those moments (how the delivery day is set, when the discount ends, where skipping lives) or a change for each, not only the customer's side.
No invented numbers, quotes or timings beyond what was supplied.

prompt: We've finished the map of how a new restaurant customer gets set up on our payroll software: 7 stages from signed contract to first successful payroll run, 4 rows (what the owner does, what our onboarding specialist does, what the software does, and what happens out of sight like bank verification), an emotion line, 11 pain points and 9 ideas. Thursday I show it to the 12 people in the room (support, product, sales, onboarding), and the week after to our exec team in a 10-minute slot. How should I show it each time? Slides, big printout, doc? What goes on each?
rubric: Recommends a different form for each audience instead of one artifact for both.
For Thursday, a large shared view of the whole sequence (printed wall or full-width page) that people can point at and add to, with the four rows kept in the same time order.
For the exec slot, a short story built around two or three moments and their ideas, not all 11 pain points and 9 ideas, and says what to cut.
Says to attach each idea to the moment it fixes, and ends the exec version with a decision or ask.
Practical and brief enough to act on; does not redesign the map itself.

prompt:
This is the opportunities list from our workshop for a dental practice. It reads vague to me and the owner won't fund "improve communication". Can you tighten it? I don't want to lose anything the team came up with.

1. Improve communication with patients
2. Better onboarding for new patients
3. Reduce wait times
4. Make the reminders smarter
5. Enhance the billing experience
6. More personalised care
7. Fix the forms
8. Follow up after treatments

What was on the workshop wall: patients get a text reminder 48 hours before, but it doesn't say which dentist or which of our two locations. New patients fill in a 4-page paper form in the waiting room, and that's where most of the wait at first visits comes from. Insurance estimates only get explained at the desk after treatment. There's no check-in call after a filling or crown.
rubric: Keeps all eight items in some form; none is dropped or silently merged away.

Rewrites each into a specific change tied to a moment and the person it helps, using the wall details supplied (reminder without dentist or location, paper form, insurance explained after treatment, no follow-up call).
Where the context does not say what is wrong (such as more personalised care), says so or asks, instead of inventing a cause.
Adds no invented statistics, wait times or expected savings.
Briefly suggests which few to start with or an order, and why.
